notes: Ruling slot 22 = CMLN junta of Moussa Traoré (the junta itself, not MD's generic armed-forces entry, so the army sprite is not reused). Coalition slot 13 = civilian technocrats in the CMLN government. US-RDA moved from MD slot 5 to slot 18 (African socialism, slot with starting popularity) and keeps its MD sprite; PMT kept in MD slot 19 with its sprite. Slot 5 = the dissolved US-RDA Popular Militia.

0.name: Le parti du franc
0.text:
Le parti du franc is the circle of officers, senior administrators and merchants who want the junta to tie Mali firmly back to France and the West. The Malian franc, devalued by half in 1967 under agreements with Paris, still stands outside the West African monetary union, and they press for full re-entry into the CFA franc zone.

They favour authoritarian order, anti-communism, French budget support and closer ties with Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire, while dismantling what remains of the socialist economy. They have no organisation but sit in ministries and the central bank. Their leverage lies in Paris's money and in Mali's chronic shortage of foreign exchange.

1.name: Parti progressiste soudanais
1.text:
The Sudanese Progressive Party is the conservative party of Fily Dabo Sissoko, the colonial-era deputy who led French Sudan's chiefs and notables against the US-RDA in the 1950s. Crushed at the polls in 1959 and swallowed by the one-party state, its leaders were blamed for the 1962 currency riots, and Sissoko died in detention in 1964.

Its surviving notables, freed from fear by the fall of Modibo Keïta, hope to revive a party of chiefs, landowners, merchants and Muslim elders that defends private property, close ties with France and the West, and respect for traditional authority. Its leverage lies in families who long resented the US-RDA revolution.

2.name: Les constitutionnalistes
2.text:
Les constitutionnalistes are the lawyers, teachers, magistrates and liberal civil servants who welcomed the fall of Modibo Keïta in November 1968 as the end of the one-party state and now hold the junta to its promise of a return to constitutional rule. They meet in Bamako's professional associations, newspaper offices and parish halls.

They want a written constitution, multiparty elections, an independent judiciary, press freedom and the release of political prisoners, along with a mixed economy and good relations with the West. Without arms or masses, they rely on argument. Their leverage lies in the regime's need for respectability with donors and in the support of the educated elite.

3.name: Union nationale des travailleurs du Mali
3.english: National Union of Workers of Mali
3.native_full: Union nationale des travailleurs du Mali
3.text:
The National Union of Workers of Mali is the single trade-union centre founded in 1963, uniting civil servants, teachers, railwaymen and workers of the state enterprises. Closely tied to the US-RDA under Keïta, it survived the 1968 coup, but its leaders are under pressure as the junta trims state payrolls and purges the old party's supporters.

It defends wages, jobs in the state companies, union freedom and social security, and increasingly argues for an elected civilian government with a reformist, social-democratic programme. Its leverage lies in the public sector: a strike by teachers or railwaymen can paralyse Bamako and the Dakar–Niger line.
3.wiki: National Union of Workers of Mali

4.name: Les boursiers de Moscou
4.text:
Les boursiers de Moscou are the Malian engineers, doctors, officers and teachers trained in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe during the Keïta years, when Mali was one of Moscow's closest partners in Africa. Hundreds now work in ministries and state companies, and Soviet advisers still serve with the army and in geology and aviation.

They want the junta to keep Soviet military cooperation, preserve the planned economy and the state enterprises, and in time return to a socialist path guided by scientific socialism. Some are close to the clandestine Malian Party of Labour, others are simply careerists. Their leverage lies in technical skills the state cannot do without.

5.name: Milice populaire
5.text:
The Popular Militia was the armed youth organisation of the US-RDA, which in 1967–68 policed markets, searched homes and humiliated officers during Modibo Keïta's 'active revolution'. Its abuses helped provoke the army coup of November 1968, after which it was disbanded and many of its leaders were arrested.

Its surviving cadres, scattered among youth groups and the unemployed, remain committed to a radical, collectivist revolution against merchants, chiefs and 'reactionary' officers, and to close ties with China, Cuba and the Soviet Union. They are hunted by the security services. Their leverage lies in grievance, in underground cells and in the memory of power.

6.name: Les modibistes
6.text:
Les modibistes are the loyalists of Modibo Keïta, held in the desert at Kidal since the coup of 19 November 1968 together with many of his former ministers. Old party barons, former political commissioners and veterans of the independence struggle, they refuse to accept the junta and dream of restoring the Keïta order.

Unlike the radicals of the militia, they are guardians of the party hierarchy and discipline, hostile to French influence and Western capital and nostalgic for the one-party state that ruled through committees. They want Keïta's release above all. Their leverage lies in old networks in Bamako's quarters and in the prestige of the father of independence.

7.name: Sûreté nationale
7.text:
The National Security Service is the police and intelligence apparatus that the CMLN has turned into its chief instrument of control, directed by Captain Tiécoro Bagayoko, one of the young officers of the 1968 coup. It watches former US-RDA cadres, unions, students and fellow officers, and runs the detention system that holds Keïta's ministers.

Its chiefs believe in a hard, centralised state ruled by the military without civilian interference, suspicious of the West and keen to keep socialist-era controls that give them patronage. They are feared rather than loved. Their leverage lies in files, informers and the power to arrest anyone in the country.

8.name: Les négociants libanais
8.text:
Les négociants libanais are the Lebanese merchant families of Bamako, Kayes, Mopti and Ségou, largely Shia from south Lebanon, who are returning to wholesale and transport trade as the junta loosens Keïta's state monopolies. They keep a low political profile and depend on the goodwill of officials.

In religious matters they follow the reformist Imam Musa al-Sadr, who seeks emigrant support for the Shia community of Lebanon. Politically they want liberalised trade, a convertible currency and protection from arbitrary arrest and confiscation. Their leverage lies in capital, import-export networks reaching Dakar and Abidjan, and loans that officers and officials quietly need.

9.name: La Husayniyya de Bamako
9.text:
La Husayniyya de Bamako is a small circle of devout Lebanese Shia who gather in a private house for prayers and the mourning of Ashura under the guidance of men schooled in Najaf. They keep apart from the trading notables of their own community, whom they consider too worldly.

They hold that society should be guided by learned jurists and that Muslims must resist Western moral influence. They play no role in Malian politics and stay clear of the security services, concentrating on the religious education of their children. Their leverage is tiny: family money and ties to clerical networks in Iraq and Lebanon.

10.name: Les Kunta
10.text:
Les Kunta are the great Arab-Berber scholarly lineage of Timbuktu and the Azawad, heirs of the Qadiri saint Sidi al-Mukhtar al-Kunti, whose religious authority spans Mali, Mauritania and Niger. With the imams of Timbuktu's ancient mosques and other marabout families, they form the conservative Islamic establishment of the north.

They are quietist and loyal to the state, provided it respects religious scholars, Koranic schools and customary justice among the nomads. They welcomed the end of Keïta's campaigns against 'feudalism'. Their leverage lies in their religious prestige among Arabs, Tuareg and Songhay, and in their mediation between Bamako and the northern tribes.

11.name: Les héritiers d'El Hadj Omar
11.english: The Heirs of El Hadj Omar
11.text:
Les héritiers d'El Hadj Omar are the descendants and followers of the Tijani jihad leader Umar Tall, whose nineteenth-century Islamic state stretched from the Senegal River to Ségou and Bandiagara before the French conquest. Among the Tukulor families of Nioro, Ségou and Bandiagara, a minority keeps alive the dream of a state governed by the sharia.

Its most ardent members reject the secular republic, its French law codes and its soldiers, and speak of restoring a caliphate under Islamic law across the Sahel. They have no organisation and little following beyond old families. Their leverage lies in the prestige of the jihad and in religious lineages.

12.name: Union culturelle musulmane
12.text:
The Muslim Cultural Union is the reformist association founded in Dakar in 1953 by Cheikh Touré, which took root among Bamako's Wahhabi-leaning merchants and teachers. Restricted under Modibo Keïta, who distrusted its independence and its links abroad, it is reviving under the junta through its Arabic schools and mosques.

It calls for a purified Islam free of saint veneration, modern Arabic-language education, Muslim morality in public life and political participation within the law, in a spirit close to the Muslim Brotherhood and Egyptian reformism. Its leverage lies in merchant money and in the graduates of its medersas.

13.name: Les technocrates de Koulouba
13.text:
Les technocrates de Koulouba are the civilian ministers, planners and senior civil servants whom the CMLN keeps in government to run the state from the presidential hill of Koulouba. Many served under Keïta, but they now manage the junta's retreat from his planned economy, negotiating with France, the IMF and other donors.

They favour pragmatic, non-aligned government: gradual liberalisation of trade, reform of loss-making state companies, budgets balanced with outside help and a cautious return to civilian institutions. They do not challenge the officers' primacy. Their leverage lies in their expertise and in the fact that no donor will deal with soldiers alone.

14.name: Les notables de Ségou
14.text:
Les notables de Ségou are the village chiefs, lineage heads and landowning families of the Bambara heartland along the Niger, whose authority Keïta's party committees tried to break in the name of socialism. Since the coup they have recovered much of their standing, and the junta relies on them to collect taxes and keep order.

They want an end to compulsory collective fields and grain deliveries, respect for custom, chieftaincy and Islam, and a government that stays out of village affairs and out of the blocs. Their leverage lies in the countryside, where peasants still follow them, and in the regime's need for rural peace.

15.name: Chambre de commerce du Mali
15.text:
The Chamber of Commerce of Mali speaks for the great merchant families of Bamako, Kayes and Mopti, the French and Lebanese import houses and the transporters who move goods between Dakar, Abidjan and the Niger. Sidelined by Keïta's state trading company SOMIEX, they see the junta's liberalisation as their opportunity.

They want SOMIEX's monopolies dismantled, private trade restored, the Malian franc made convertible and good relations with France and the franc zone. Pragmatic and wealthy, they finance officers and officials when needed. Their leverage lies in capital, credit and the import trade on which supplies to the towns depend.

16.name: Les commerçants du 20 juillet
16.text:
Les commerçants du 20 juillet are the small traders of Bamako's markets who rioted on 20 July 1962 against the creation of the Malian franc and the state's trade monopolies. Their protest was crushed and blamed on the PSP leaders, but its memory endures, and many now feel vindicated by the coup.

They want free markets, free movement of goods across the borders with Senegal, Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire, low taxes and the end of price controls and SOMIEX quotas. Wary of politics, they back whoever leaves trade alone. Their leverage lies in the markets and in the smuggling routes that feed the towns.

17.name: Service des eaux et forêts
17.text:
The Water and Forests Service is the corps of foresters and rangers, inherited from the French colonial administration, that guards Mali's classified forests, wildlife reserves and fragile Sahelian pastures. Its uniformed agents are feared in the villages for fines on wood-cutting and bush fires, but they see themselves as the last line against the desert.

They call for reforestation, control of grazing and charcoal burning, protection of wildlife in the Boucle du Baoulé and conservation of the Niger's waters. Technocratic and apolitical, they welcome development aid from any bloc. Their leverage lies in their legal powers and in growing alarm at the advancing Sahara.

18.name: Union soudanaise–Rassemblement démocratique africain
18.text:
The Sudanese Union–African Democratic Rally is the party of Modibo Keïta that led Mali to independence in 1960 and ruled it as a single party until the army coup of 19 November 1968. Its organs dissolved by the CMLN, it survives underground in neighbourhoods, unions and schools, while Keïta and his leading ministers are held in detention in the north.

Its programme is African socialism: state planning, cooperatives, public enterprises, a national currency and a non-aligned foreign policy friendly to the Soviet Union, China and Guinea. Its base lies among urban workers, teachers and veterans of the independence struggle. Its leverage lies in its legitimacy and residual organisation.

19.name: Parti malien du travail
19.text:
The Malian Party of Labour is a clandestine Marxist party formed in the mid-1960s by former members of the African Independence Party who found the US-RDA's socialism too timid and too bureaucratic. Small and secretive, it recruits among teachers, students and young civil servants and now operates under the eye of the junta's security services.

It stands for a genuine workers' and peasants' revolution, scientific socialism adapted to African conditions and independence from all great powers, criticising both Moscow's line and Keïta's party elite. Its leverage lies in its disciplined cadres in schools and unions, whose influence reaches well beyond their numbers.

20.name: Le Mali d'abord
20.text:
Le Mali d'abord is the populist mood of townspeople, demobilised soldiers, small traders and peasants who cheered the coup of November 1968 as liberation from the militia and the party commissars. They want the officers to clean house, punish the old barons and put ordinary Malians first.

They are nationalist and suspicious of foreigners, from Lebanese merchants to Soviet advisers and French experts, and they demand cheap grain, jobs and law and order. Many voice resentment of educated elites and politicians of every kind. Their leverage lies in crowds that can be brought onto the streets of Bamako, Ségou and Kayes.

21.name: Les officiers de Kati
21.text:
Les officiers de Kati are the hardline officers of the Kati garrison and military school, where the coup of November 1968 was prepared by Lieutenant Moussa Traoré and his fellow junior officers. They insist that the army must rule as long as it sees fit, with no timetable for a return to civilian government.

They want a disciplined, militarised nation, the eradication of the US-RDA, strict censorship and the army as sole guardian of Mali's unity and honour, including against unrest among the Tuareg of the north. They despise politicians and distrust foreign advisers. Their leverage lies in the troops at Kati, a short drive from Bamako.

22.name: Comité militaire de libération nationale
22.text:
The Military Committee for National Liberation is the junta of fourteen officers that overthrew Modibo Keïta on 19 November 1968. Led by Moussa Traoré, a lieutenant at the time of the coup, as president of the committee and head of state, it governs by ordinance through a mixed military and civilian government, promising a return to democratic rule once the economy recovers.

The committee abolished the militia and the party organs, loosened state control of trade and seeks better relations with France and the West while keeping Soviet arms. It is nationalist, pragmatic and authoritarian, held together by fear of the old party. Its leverage is total: it holds the army, police and state.

23.name: Aménokal des Kel Adagh
23.text:
The Amenokal of the Kel Adagh is the paramount chief of the Tuareg confederation of the Adrar des Ifoghas around Kidal, an office held by Attaher ag Illi of the Ifoghas lineage. The chieftaincy survived colonial rule and the Kel Adagh revolt of 1963–64, which Keïta's army crushed harshly, and the junta now leans on the amenokal to keep the north quiet.

It stands for the hereditary authority of the noble lineages, Islamic law and custom, pastoral freedom and autonomy from the southern state. It neither seeks independence nor trusts Bamako. Its leverage lies in clan loyalties across the Adrar and in its role as the state's indispensable intermediary.
